quotes.quote: Pitchblack racing snail (Neritina pulligera). Origin: Thailand.

It is found in South India, Seychelles, Madagascar, Thailand, Indonesia, northwestern Australia, Celebes, New Guinea, New Caledonia, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Philippines, Japan, and the eastern coast of Africa from Kenya to South Africa.

sections.html:
• Name: Black Military Helmet Snail
  • Other names: Black nerite snail, Baseball cap nerite, Red lipped nerite, Dusky nerite, Black Racer Nerite Snail
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: very difficult
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: from dark olive to almost black

Neritina pulligera is one of the best algae-eating snails in the hobby. It is peaceful, easy to care for and low-maintenance, so it can be recommended even to beginners. It is mostly herbivorous and eats algae and biofilm, which reduces cleaning work in the tank.

Neritina pulligera is widely distributed in the Indo-Pacific region (excluding French Polynesia). It is found in South India, Seychelles, Madagascar, Thailand, Indonesia, northwestern Australia, Celebes, New Guinea, New Caledonia, Solomon Islands, Fiji, Philippines, Japan, and the eastern coast of Africa from Kenya to South Africa.
It is a freshwater gastropod, generally found in clear, coastal, fast-flowing freshwater streams and small rivers with rocky substrates.

These snails do not need much space, but 20 litres is the absolute minimum, for three reasons:

  • In anything smaller there may be feeding problems, as there will not be enough algae and biofilm.
  • Stable water parameters are hard to keep in smaller tanks, even for experienced aquarists.
  • They live in rivers with relatively fast water flow, which is hard to replicate in small tanks.

40 litres is the optimal tank size for 2–3 snails.

They do not come out of the water often, but it is still recommended to lower the waterline by 2.5–5 cm and/or use a tight-fitting cover to stop them crawling out.

This species can adapt to unfavourable and fluctuating habitats, but does much better in a tank set up around its needs. The tank should be cycled and fully established before the snails are added; check the water with a test kit.

Lighting: snails are nocturnal and indifferent to it; adapt the lighting to the needs of plants (and/or algae).

Substrate: smooth gravel and rocks are best, as they favour algae growth.

Decorations: driftwood, PVC pipes, leaves, rocks, live and fake plants all provide surface for algae and biofilm, so any decor is a good choice.

Acclimation: do not drop them straight into the tank. Sudden changes can harm them. As with all invertebrates, acclimate them very slowly to avoid unnecessary stress.

Temperature: 22–28 °C, ideally 24–26 °C.

pH: 7.0–8.0, in hard water. The thick shell lets them tolerate slightly acidic water (pH 6.5), but this is not recommended, as acidic water slowly dissolves the shell (usually as tiny holes).

Hardness: fairly hard to very hard water (8–30 GH). They survive in soft water, although this may eventually be detrimental.

Nitrate: below 40 ppm.

Filtration: no special requirements; any filter suited to the tank size is fine.

Water flow and aeration: these snails appreciate fast currents and high oxygen levels. In the wild, river water velocity is about 0.5 m/s. A suitably sized pump is needed to move the water and oxygenate the tank. Their lifespan can be reduced in suboptimal conditions, which is why bigger tanks are preferred if you want them to live longer than a few months.

They are primarily herbivorous. In the wild they mostly eat algae and biofilm on rocks and plants, so keep live plants in the tank to encourage algae growth, and leaves for biofilm. They are one of few nerite species (besides Horned Nerite snails) that may even eat black beard algae.

Slow-growing large-leaved plants such as Anubias, Cryptocoryne and Java fern are ideal. They can be too heavy for grass-like plants such as dwarf hairgrass and Pogostemon quadrifolius.

Do not rely on their scavenging alone to survive (unless the tank is huge and full of algae), as they may starve. Supplement with other foods:

  • Blanched vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, carrot, cucumber, lettuce, corn, spinach, peas, squash, leafy greens, etc.).
  • Fruits (sweet apple, banana, pear, melon, mango, etc.).
  • Leaves.

Calcium is vital for snails, most obviously for shell formation.

Diet type: mostly herbivore/omnivore. Food preference: algae. Feeding frequency: 2–3 times a week.

Feeding problems: some aquarists report that their snails eat nothing but algae and biofilm, which becomes a problem once the tank is clean. Algae can be grown on rocks in a separate container:

  • Use any transparent container (large bottle, spare tank, etc.).
  • Fill it with water from water changes.
  • Add many small, clean, aquarium-safe rocks such as marble chips and ceramic filter media.
  • Leave it under the strongest lighting available, ideally 24/7.
  • Optional: add a fertiliser for plants and/or an airstone to boost algae growth.
  • Once the rocks turn green, place a few in the tank for the snails, then repeat.

Keep training the snails to eat algae wafers and vegetables, giving them time to learn these are food.

Plant safety: they are safe in planted tanks. They only graze on plant surfaces and have no interest in eating live plants.
Like its close relative, the Zebra snail Neritina turrita, this snail is an excellent algae eater.

They are non-aggressive, solitary and very shy, and need a calm environment and peaceful tank mates. Like most snails they are nocturnal; activity starts at dusk and gradually stops before sunrise, mainly to avoid visual predators while feeding. At dusk, algae hold maximum nutrients at the end of the photosynthetic period, which suits grazers.

They are not natural diggers; even if they can burrow in soft substrate, they do not move under it.

When disturbed or threatened they close the shell completely with the operculum, and it may take time before they move again.

Social: no. Active: at night. Peaceful: yes. Burrower: no.
Experience with this snail is that they do not leave the water, in contrast to other species of the genus.

Black Military Helmet snail reaches about 4 cm in length, 3 cm in width and 2.5 cm in aperture height; on average shells are 2.5–3 cm long. The shell is dark brown, almost black, or sometimes olive-ish, thick and orbicularly ovate with an expanded aperture. The aperture is orange with a white edge. The body is dark with white spots. The columellar area is bluish-black on the outer half, fading toward the inner half. A deep orange band runs along the inner margin of the outer lip. The parietal wall is flat, black-greyish, but may vary towards yellowish. The operculum is greenish-yellow with dark spiral bands.

Black Military Helmet snails are not successfully bred in captivity. All available animals are wild-caught, which poses a potential biohazard and depletes natural populations. No successful breeding in laboratory conditions has been reported either. They need brackish water to breed and do not reproduce in freshwater.

The scarce scientific information says:

  • Neritidae have internal fertilisation and encapsulate their eggs afterwards.
  • Females can store sperm from males, which permits continuous spawning.
  • Eggs are protected in a hard capsule, relatively large (1.4–1.8 mm long).
  • Each capsule contains 200 to 300 embryos (veliger larvae).
  • Females deposit clusters of 4–39 egg capsules, with about 10 minutes between ovipositions.
  • Capsules are usually attached to rocky substrate and to the shells of other snails.
  • In nature, females release free-swimming veligers into freshwater, where the current sweeps them into brackish lagoons or the open sea.
  • The veligers remain in marine plankton for at least several weeks, completing metamorphosis into small copies of the adults.
  • The larvae cannot develop in freshwater.
  • The veligers feed on microplankton (phyto- and zooplankton).

By laying capsules on the shells of other snails, they increase their survival rate. The eggs and markings eventually dissolve in freshwater.
The species does not breed in the aquarium.

Taxonomy: it is still incompletely understood. The species reportedly shows large morphological variability with several sub-species. According to some scientists, about 40 taxa are considered synonyms of Neritina pulligera; for example Neritina petitii, Neritina canalis and Neritina knorri are considered varieties or used as junior synonyms.

Etymology: Nerites comes from ancient Greek Νηρίτης, meaning 'sea snail'. Pulligerus comes from the Latin 'pullus' (young, or dark-coloured) and 'gero' (wearing or carrying), so the name translates roughly as 'the dark-coloured sea snail'.

Lifespan: there is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. With appropriate care they live 4–5 years in the aquarium, depending on feeding, poor living conditions and shipment stress.

Pros: beautiful, excellent algae eaters, great cleaners, peaceful, do not eat plants. Cons: need brackish water to breed, can climb out of tanks, do not reproduce in freshwater, require good water flow.
